paras: The attempted lynching of Sam Jernagan was a failed attempt by a mob in Trinity County, Texas, in the summer of 1915 to lynch a Black prisoner charged with assaulting a white girl. Sheriff Thornton moved Jernagan to the jail at Houston, and in August state troops guarded him at his trial in Groveton, where he was convicted and sentenced to death. Texas editorials held up the sheriff's refusal to yield to the mob as an example for other officers.

Jernagan, described in the wire reports as "a negro," was charged with criminal assault on Rosa Vondra, a fourteen-year-old white girl. An editorial first printed in the Houston Post dated the charge to June 17, though the opening of the reprinted text is damaged.

According to the Laredo Weekly Times, a mob attempted to lynch the prisoner some time after his arrest, but Sheriff Thornton took him toward Houston instead. On the way Jernagan escaped; he was recaptured the same night, taken to Houston and lodged in jail. A wire report confirmed that the sheriff had sent him to the Harris County jail "for safe keeping."

Expecting violence at the trial, the sheriff asked the governor for military protection, which was granted at once. On August 9 about sixty state troops, infantry and cavalry under Captain Dallas J. Matthews, left Houston with Jernagan for Groveton. A later weekly item named the units as thirty men of the Houston Cavalry under Captain Roy Blount and thirty of the Houston Light Guard under Matthews, but gave their departure as Sunday.

At Groveton on August 12 a jury found Jernagan guilty and he was sentenced to death, the conviction resting on his confession; he did not take the stand. Soldiers guarded the courthouse during the trial, and one dispatch reported that the court room applauded the verdict but that "there was no other demonstration." No report of arrests of mob members, an appeal or an execution appears in the coverage.

The case reached the white press mainly through Associated Press dispatches from Houston, carried in Bryan, Brownsville, Waxahachie, Laredo and Oklahoma papers between August 9 and 15. Headlines focused on the soldiers, such as "State Troops Guard Negro Prisoner" in Bryan and "Troopers Save Black" in Oklahoma City. The Daily Ardmoreite instead headed its verdict story "Death Penalty for Jernigan, Black Fiend."

Editorials gave the episode its larger meaning. The Houston Post, reprinted in Corpus Christi, commended Thornton for sparing "a good old county" the "disgrace of a lynching" and argued that most lynchings could be prevented if sheriffs did their duty. The Laredo Weekly Times, citing the Galveston News, called his conduct "A Good Example" and argued there was "no excuse for the lynching of a man accused of such a crime," since such a defendant would not escape the courts. No coverage of the case in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Sam Jernagan
bases: A mob attempted to lynch a Black prisoner accused of assaulting a white girl; the sheriff kept him from it and state troops guarded his trial (A10, A9, A7).
No one was killed: the mob's attempt failed and Jernagan was tried and sentenced to death in court (A10, A4); the mob, of unstated size, acted on the assault accusation (A10).

Only the Laredo editorial describes the mob's attempt and the escape (A10); the Houston Post editorial and a wire variant speak of the danger of a lynching (A9, A7), while the troop escort, trial and sentence are confirmed by independent AP reports (A1, A2, A4).

accounts.label: Laredo Weekly Times editorial
accounts.gist: A mob tried to lynch the prisoner; the sheriff took him toward Houston, he escaped en route, was recaptured that night, and was later tried at Groveton under troop guard.

accounts.label: Houston Post editorial
accounts.gist: The sheriff, seeing the danger of violence, asked the governor for military protection so the county would be spared 'the disgrace of a lynching'.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Sixty state troops took Jernagan from Houston to Groveton at the sheriff's request; he was convicted on his confession and sentenced to death under guard.

framing.detail: The Houston Post and Laredo editorials condemned 'mob law' and praised Sheriff Thornton's 'duty', arguing that an accused 'brute' would not escape the courts, so a lynching had no excuse.
AP stories ran under headlines such as 'State Troops Guard Negro Prisoner' and 'Troopers Save Black'.
The Daily Ardmoreite headlined the verdict 'Death Penalty for Jernigan, Black Fiend'.

conflicts.note: The dated AP dispatches are better evidence than the undated weekly item, which may have been written from a different report.
The verdict story is more specific; the editorials also say 'a girl' (A9, A10).
